subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 26-year-old man is running a marathon and relies heavily on muscle glycogen for energy. During the race his blood glucose remains stable even though his muscles are rapidly consuming glucose-6-phosphate.
question: Which of the following best explains why muscle glycogen cannot directly maintain blood glucose during this exercise?
explanation_correct: Muscle glycogen is degraded to glucose-6-phosphate, which enters glycolysis because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and cannot release free glucose into the blood. The liver, which possesses glucose-6-phosphatase, is the organ that maintains blood glucose during fasting and exercise.

explanation_incorrect.A: Muscle contains abundant glycogen phosphorylase, which is why muscle glycogen can be mobilized during exercise.
explanation_incorrect.B: Muscle contains both debranching enzyme activities and can fully degrade branched glycogen to glucose-6-phosphate.
explanation_incorrect.D: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase is a gluconeogenic enzyme; its absence is not the reason muscle glycogen cannot raise blood glucose, since muscle also cannot release glucose-6-phosphate.
explanation_incorrect.E: Glucagon does not act on muscle, but muscle glycogenolysis is driven by epinephrine and contraction, so receptor status is not the explanation.

educationalObjective: Muscle glycogen cannot raise blood glucose because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so its glucose-6-phosphate is used locally in glycolysis.
